idiom_name: strong typedef class (explicit constructor + private member)
implementation_notes: The default C++ realization: a class with one private member, an explicit constructor that validates, a named accessor and the operators the domain actually needs (==, <=>, hashing, operator<<). This is what the pattern costs in C++: the language gives distinctness for free but no boilerplate removal, so each type is a short, deliberate class. Prefer value semantics (pass by value, immutable member) and add only the operators the domain wants.
pitfalls: An implicit converting constructor (or a public member) silently reopens the hole: keep the constructor explicit and the member private.
Without a std::hash specialization (or std::less/<=>) the type cannot be an unordered_map key and ordered containers fall back to address comparison.
operator== alone does not order: add <=> (C++20) or operator< when the type lands in std::set/std::map.

variants.name: Opaque identifier as scoped enumeration
variants.implementation_notes: For integral identifiers that carry no arithmetic meaning, a scoped enumeration with a fixed underlying type is the whole wrapper: an enumeration is already a distinct type in C++, comparison and hashing work out of the box, and an empty enumerator list makes the type opaque (no enumerator names leak). Conversion helpers turn the raw integer into the id and back; the fixed underlying type pins the ABI and serialized width. Choose this when the value is only ever compared, stored and passed - not when it needs methods or string validation.
pitfalls: Once cast to the underlying type the value is an ordinary integer again, so keep static_cast inside the conversion helpers and out of business code.
An enumeration without a fixed underlying type may be int-sized; always state the underlying type before the value reaches a wire format or ABI.
Scoped enumerations cannot carry invariants (no constructor), so validation has to happen in the factory function that returns the enum.

variants.name: BOOST_STRONG_TYPEDEF macro
variants.implementation_notes: Boost.Serialization ships the macro that named the idiom: it expands to a wrapper type plus the full relational and arithmetic operator set, giving a drop-in strong typedef where the hand-written class would only repeat boilerplate (and where the underlying type's operators are all wanted). Use it when Boost is already a dependency and the wrapper is a thin token; avoid it when the domain forbids arithmetic, because the generated operators permit it.
variants.code_sketch:
#include <boost/serialization/strong_typedef.hpp>

BOOST_STRONG_TYPEDEF(int, user_id)
BOOST_STRONG_TYPEDEF(int, order_id)

void f(user_id);   // f(order_id{}) does not compile
pitfalls: The macro generates arithmetic operators as well as comparisons, so user_id + user_id (and worse) compiles; wrap it in your own factory when the domain forbids arithmetic.
It pulls a serialization library into the model layer, and the generated type's behaviour is documented by Boost, not by your code - a maintenance dependency.
